1 Methodology

1.1 Doubly-Robust Estimation via the IPS Covariate

ForestSearch’s propensity score (PS) adjustment follows the doubly-robust methodology of Bang & Robins (2005). The key idea: include the inverse propensity score (IPS) as a covariate in the outcome model. This is distinct from inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting (IPTW).

For each subject \(i\) with estimated propensity score \(\hat{e}(X_i) = \hat{P}(W_i = 1 \mid X_i)\):

\[ \text{IPS}_i = \begin{cases} 1 / \hat{e}(X_i) & \text{if } W_i = 1 \text{ (treated)} \\ 1 / (1 - \hat{e}(X_i)) & \text{if } W_i = 0 \text{ (control)} \end{cases} \]

The outcome model becomes:

\[ g\bigl(E[Y_i \mid W_i, \text{IPS}_i]\bigr) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 W_i + \beta_2 \text{IPS}_i \]

where \(g(\cdot)\) is the link function (log for Poisson/IRR, logit for OR, identity for RD). The treatment coefficient \(\hat\beta_1\) is the doubly-robust treatment effect estimate: it is consistent if either the propensity model or the outcome model is correctly specified, but not necessarily both.

1.2 Why IPS Covariate, Not IPTW

Property IPS Covariate IPTW
Model glm(Y ~ treat + ips_covar) glm(Y ~ treat, weights = 1/e(x))
Extreme PS Absorbed by coefficient Inflates variance
Small subgroups Stable (just another covariate) Unstable (extreme weights)
Doubly-robust Yes (Bang & Robins 2005) Only with augmentation (AIPW)

For ForestSearch, the IPS covariate approach is preferred because the estimator closure is called repeatedly on small subgroup slices (down to n.min = 60). IPTW with extreme weights in small samples would be highly unstable.

2 Complete Workflow

2.1 Stage 1: GRF Screening (Internal PS)

When use_grf = TRUE, GRF fits causal_forest(X, Y, W) which internally estimates \(\hat{e}(X_i) = E[W_i \mid X_i]\) via regression_forest(X, W). These out-of-bag, cross-fitted propensity scores are used within GRF for:

  • Residualization: \(\tilde{W}_i = W_i - \hat{e}(X_i)\)
  • Doubly-robust CATE scores: The AIPW construction in double_robust_scores()
  • Variable importance: Splits that explain treatment heterogeneity

The PS at this stage is used only for candidate factor selection — it does not affect the downstream effect estimates. For RCTs, W.hat = 0.5 is passed (known randomization probability), so PS estimation is skipped.

causal_forest(X, Y, W, W.hat = 0.5)  # RCT
causal_forest(X, Y, W)                # Observational (W.hat estimated)
     ↓
double_robust_scores()  →  policy_tree()  →  candidate cuts

2.2 Stage 2: PS Estimation for Effect Adjustment

Location: forestsearch_main.R, Section 2C

After the outcome type and effect measure are resolved (Section 2B), ForestSearch optionally estimates propensity scores on the full df.analysis and constructs the IPS covariate.

forestsearch(..., ps_method = "grf", is.RCT = FALSE)
     ↓
  Section 2C: estimate_propensity_scores()
     ├── Estimate e(X) on full sample via GRF/LASSO/logistic
     ├── Trim PS to [2.5%, 97.5%]
     ├── Compute IPS covariate:
     │     W=1: 1/e(X)
     │     W=0: 1/(1-e(X))
     ├── Add ps_hat and ips_covar columns to df.analysis
     └── Rebuild estimator closure:
           make_effect_estimator(..., adjust_covariates = "ips_covar")

Default behavior:

Setting ps_method IPS included Rationale
is.RCT = TRUE "none" No Randomization ensures balance
is.RCT = FALSE "grf" Yes Non-parametric, cross-fitted
User-supplied ps_hat = vec Yes Maximum flexibility

2.3 Stage 3: Subgroup Search

Location: subgroup_search.R → subgroup.consistency.R

The estimator closure (now containing adjust_covariates = "ips_covar") is called on each candidate subgroup slice during the search and consistency evaluation:

for each candidate subgroup S:
  df_slice <- df[df$candidate_var <= cutpoint, ]
     ↓
  estimator_fn(df_slice)
     → glm(Y ~ treat + ips_covar, data = df_slice, ...)
     → returns list(estimate, se, converged, ...)

Critical detail: The ips_covar values within each slice are the full-sample IPS values for those observations. The propensity scores are never re-estimated within subgroup slices. This is correct because:

  1. \(P(W = 1 \mid X)\) is a design quantity — it reflects the treatment assignment mechanism for the entire study, not a subgroup property.
  2. Subgroup slices can be small (\(n = 60\)). Re-estimating a PS model with 7 covariates on 60 observations would be unstable.
  3. Conditioning on the subgroup would violate the positivity assumption within slices and change the estimand.

2.4 Stage 4: Consistency Evaluation

Location: subgroup.consistency.R

For each candidate subgroup that passes the screening threshold, the consistency pipeline:

  1. Splits the subgroup 50/50 randomly, fs.splits times
  2. Applies the estimator closure to each half-sample
  3. Checks whether both halves show treatment harm (\(\hat\beta_1 \geq\) hr.consistency)

The IPS covariate flows through unchanged — each half-sample contains the original full-sample IPS values for its members.

2.5 Stage 5: Bootstrap Bias Correction

Location: bootstrap_analysis_dofuture.R

The bootstrap has two distinct evaluations, each with different PS handling:

2.5.1 Evaluation A: Original Subgroup on Bootstrap Data

df_boot <- df_boot_analysis[sample(N, N, replace = TRUE), ]
df_H <- subset(df_boot, treat.recommend == 0)
     ↓
estimator_fn(df_H)   # Uses ORIGINAL IPS values, resampled

The estimator closure (with adjust_covariates = "ips_covar") is applied to the resampled data. The ips_covar column is carried from the original data — resampled subjects bring their original IPS values.

2.5.2 Evaluation B: Re-Selection (New Subgroup from Bootstrap Data)

args_FS_boot <- fs.est$args_call_all
args_FS_boot$df.analysis <- dfnew_boot   # bootstrap-resampled data
     ↓
do.call(forestsearch, args_FS_boot)
     ↓
  Section 2C re-entered:
    estimate_propensity_scores(dfnew_boot, ..., method = "grf")
    → FRESH PS estimated on bootstrap-resampled data
    → FRESH IPS covariate computed
    → FRESH estimator closure built

When forestsearch() is called on bootstrap data, it re-enters Section 2C and re-estimates the propensity score on the resampled data. This is methodologically correct: the bootstrap should replicate the entire estimation procedure, including PS estimation.

2.6 Stage 6: Summary Tables and Visualization

Location: summary_utility_functions.R

SG_tab_estimates_glm() and format_bootstrap_table_gt() use the estimator closure to compute subgroup-level effect estimates for display. The closure carries the adjust_covariates setting, so all displayed estimates are doubly-robust when PS adjustment is active.

3 PS Estimation Methods

3.1 GRF (regression_forest)

df <- survival::gbsg
df$id <- seq_len(nrow(df))
df$grade3 <- as.integer(df$grade == "3")
confs <- c("age", "meno", "size", "grade3", "nodes", "pgr", "er")

# GRF PS estimation
ps_grf <- estimate_propensity_scores(df, "hormon", confs, method = "grf")

cat("GRF regression_forest PS:\n")
#> GRF regression_forest PS:
cat("  N:", length(ps_grf$ps_hat), "\n")
#>   N: 686
cat("  Mean PS:", round(mean(ps_grf$ps_hat), 4), "\n")
#>   Mean PS: 0.3588
cat("  SD:", round(sd(ps_grf$ps_hat), 4), "\n")
#>   SD: 0.1174
cat("  Range:", round(range(ps_grf$ps_hat), 4), "\n")
#>   Range: 0.1783 0.5733
cat("  Trimmed:", ps_grf$trimmed, "\n")
#>   Trimmed: 0
cat("  IPS covar range:", round(range(ps_grf$ips_covar), 2), "\n")
#>   IPS covar range: 1.22 5.61

Properties:

  • Non-parametric: adapts to complex covariate-treatment relationships
  • Cross-fitted via out-of-bag predictions (avoids overfitting)
  • Already computed when use_grf = TRUE (zero additional cost)
  • Default for observational studies

4 Simulation Study

4.1 Data-Generating Mechanism

We simulate an observational study with confounded treatment assignment, a known subgroup with treatment harm, and a prognostic confounder that also drives treatment assignment.

simulate_obs_study <- function(
    n = 2000, seed = 42L,
    confounding_strength = 1.0,    # controls strength of treatment-covariate association
    subgroup_effect = 0.8,         # log-OR for subgroup (harm)
    complement_effect = -0.4,      # log-OR for complement (benefit)
    prognostic_strength = 0.5,     # x3's effect on outcome
    n_noise = 3                    # number of noise covariates
) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # Covariates
  x1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)       # subgroup definer
  x2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)       # noise binary
  x3 <- rnorm(n)                 # confounder (affects both treatment AND outcome)
  x4 <- rnorm(n)                 # prognostic only
  noise <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_noise), n, n_noise)
  colnames(noise) <- paste0("noise", seq_len(n_noise))

  # Confounded treatment assignment
  # Treatment is more likely for patients with high x3 and x1 = 1
  lp_treat <- -0.5 + confounding_strength * (0.6 * x1 + 0.8 * x3 + 0.2 * x1 * x3)
  ps_true <- plogis(lp_treat)
  treat <- rbinom(n, 1, ps_true)

  # True subgroup: x1 == 1
  in_sg <- x1 == 1

  # Outcome model (binary event)
  # x3 is a prognostic confounder (affects outcome directly)
  lp_outcome <- -1.0 +
    prognostic_strength * x3 +     # confounding path
    0.3 * x4 +                     # prognostic only
    ifelse(in_sg, subgroup_effect, complement_effect) * treat

  event <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_outcome))

  # Follow-up time (for Poisson offset analyses)
  tte <- rexp(n, rate = 0.05) + 1

  df <- data.frame(
    id = seq_len(n), x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3 = x3, x4 = x4,
    treat = treat, event = event, tte = tte,
    in_sg = in_sg, ps_true = ps_true
  )
  df <- cbind(df, noise)
  df
}

4.3 Monte Carlo Evaluation

Show code 
n_sims <- 200
n_per_sim <- 2000

confs_sim <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4")

run_mc <- function(scenario, n_sims, n_per_sim) {
  results <- data.frame(
    sim = integer(), method = character(),
    sg_est = numeric(), co_est = numeric(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  # Expand confounders for noise variables
  all_confs <- c(confs_sim, paste0("noise", seq_len(scenario$n_noise)))

  for (s in seq_len(n_sims)) {
    df_s <- simulate_obs_study(
      n = n_per_sim, seed = s,
      confounding_strength  = scenario$confounding_strength,
      subgroup_effect       = scenario$subgroup_effect,
      complement_effect     = scenario$complement_effect,
      prognostic_strength   = scenario$prognostic_strength,
      n_noise               = scenario$n_noise
    )

    # GRF propensity scores
    ps_s <- estimate_propensity_scores(df_s, "treat", all_confs, method = "grf")
    df_s <- ps_s$data

    # Unadjusted estimator
    fn_u <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
      effect_measure = "OR")

    # IPS-adjusted estimator (Bang & Robins)
    fn_a <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
      effect_measure = "OR", adjust_covariates = "ips_covar")

    # Oracle-adjusted (true PS as covariate)
    df_s$ips_oracle <- ifelse(
      df_s$treat == 1, 1 / df_s$ps_true, 1 / (1 - df_s$ps_true))
    fn_o <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
      effect_measure = "OR", adjust_covariates = "ips_oracle")

    sg <- df_s[df_s$x1 == 1, ]
    co <- df_s[df_s$x1 == 0, ]

    res_u_sg <- fn_u(sg); res_a_sg <- fn_a(sg); res_o_sg <- fn_o(sg)
    res_u_co <- fn_u(co); res_a_co <- fn_a(co); res_o_co <- fn_o(co)

    results <- rbind(results,
      data.frame(sim = s, method = "Unadjusted",
        sg_est = res_u_sg$estimate, co_est = res_u_co$estimate),
      data.frame(sim = s, method = "DR (GRF PS)",
        sg_est = res_a_sg$estimate, co_est = res_a_co$estimate),
      data.frame(sim = s, method = "DR (Oracle PS)",
        sg_est = res_o_sg$estimate, co_est = res_o_co$estimate)
    )
  }
  results
}

# Run all scenarios
all_results <- list()
for (sc_name in names(scenarios)) {
  cat("Running scenario", sc_name, ":", scenarios[[sc_name]]$name, "...\n")
  all_results[[sc_name]] <- run_mc(scenarios[[sc_name]], n_sims, n_per_sim)
}
#> Running scenario A : Moderate confounding ...
#> Running scenario B : Strong confounding ...
#> Running scenario C : Very strong confounding + weak signal ...
#> Running scenario D : Strong confounding + many noise covariates ...
#> Running scenario E : No confounding (RCT benchmark) ...

4.4 Results Summary

summarize_scenario <- function(results, true_sg, true_co, scenario_name) {
  methods <- unique(results$method)
  rows <- list()

  for (m in methods) {
    sg <- results$sg_est[results$method == m]
    co <- results$co_est[results$method == m]

    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      Scenario = scenario_name,
      Method = m,
      SG_Mean = round(mean(sg, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      SG_Bias = round(mean(sg, na.rm = TRUE) - true_sg, 3),
      SG_RMSE = round(sqrt(mean((sg - true_sg)^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 3),
      CO_Mean = round(mean(co, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      CO_Bias = round(mean(co, na.rm = TRUE) - true_co, 3),
      CO_RMSE = round(sqrt(mean((co - true_co)^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 3),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

summary_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(scenarios), function(sc) {
  sc_def <- scenarios[[sc]]
  summarize_scenario(
    all_results[[sc]],
    true_sg = sc_def$subgroup_effect,
    true_co = sc_def$complement_effect,
    scenario_name = paste0(sc, ": ", sc_def$name)
  )
}))

gt(summary_table) |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Monte Carlo Results: Unadjusted vs. Doubly-Robust**"),
    subtitle = sprintf("%d simulations, N = %d per simulation", n_sims, n_per_sim)

  tab_spanner(label = "Subgroup {x1=1}", columns = c(SG_Mean, SG_Bias, SG_RMSE)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Complement {x1=0}", columns = c(CO_Mean, CO_Bias, CO_RMSE)) |>
  cols_label(
    Scenario = "Scenario", Method = "Method",
    SG_Mean = "Mean", SG_Bias = "Bias", SG_RMSE = "RMSE",
    CO_Mean = "Mean", CO_Bias = "Bias", CO_RMSE = "RMSE"
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    md("True subgroup log-OR varies by scenario. DR = doubly-robust (IPS covariate, Bang & Robins 2005).")
  )

5 PS Quality Diagnostics

5.1 PS Calibration Across Confounding Strengths

Show code 
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

for (sc_name in c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E")) {
  sc_def <- scenarios[[sc_name]]
  df_s <- simulate_obs_study(
    n = 2000, seed = 42L,
    confounding_strength  = sc_def$confounding_strength,
    subgroup_effect       = sc_def$subgroup_effect,
    complement_effect     = sc_def$complement_effect,
    prognostic_strength   = sc_def$prognostic_strength,
    n_noise               = sc_def$n_noise
  )
  all_confs <- c(confs_sim, paste0("noise", seq_len(sc_def$n_noise)))
  ps_s <- estimate_propensity_scores(df_s, "treat", all_confs, method = "grf")

  plot(df_s$ps_true, ps_s$ps_hat, pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
       col = ifelse(df_s$in_sg, "red", "steelblue"),
       xlab = "True PS", ylab = "GRF PS",
       main = paste0(sc_name, ": ", sc_def$name),
       cex.main = 0.8)
  abline(0, 1, col = "black", lwd = 2)
  legend("topleft",
    legend = c(sprintf("cor = %.3f", cor(df_s$ps_true, ps_s$ps_hat)),
               "Subgroup", "Complement"),
    col = c(NA, "red", "steelblue"), pch = c(NA, 16, 16),
    cex = 0.7, bty = "n")
}

6 Positivity Diagnostics

6.1 IPS Covariate Distributions

Under strong confounding, the IPS covariate can have extreme values. PS trimming (at [2.5%, 97.5%] by default) mitigates this.

Show code 
# Strong confounding scenario
df_strong <- simulate_obs_study(
  n = 2000, seed = 42L,
  confounding_strength = 2.0, prognostic_strength = 1.0,
  n_noise = 3
)
all_confs_strong <- c(confs_sim, paste0("noise", 1:3))

ps_notrim <- estimate_propensity_scores(
  df_strong, "treat", all_confs_strong, method = "grf", trim = NULL)
ps_trim <- estimate_propensity_scores(
  df_strong, "treat", all_confs_strong, method = "grf")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(ps_notrim$ips_covar, breaks = 50, col = "salmon", border = "white",
     main = "IPS Covariate (No Trimming)", xlab = "IPS", xlim = c(0, 50))
abline(v = median(ps_notrim$ips_covar), col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(ps_trim$ips_covar, breaks = 50, col = "lightblue", border = "white",
     main = "IPS Covariate (Trimmed [2.5%, 97.5%])",
     xlab = "IPS", xlim = c(0, 50))
abline(v = median(ps_trim$ips_covar), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
Show code

cat("Without trimming: IPS range [",
    round(min(ps_notrim$ips_covar), 1), ",",
    round(max(ps_notrim$ips_covar), 1), "]\n")
#> Without trimming: IPS range [ 1 , 38.1 ]
Show code

    round(min(ps_trim$ips_covar), 1), ",",
    round(max(ps_trim$ips_covar), 1), "]\n")
#> With trimming:    IPS range [ 1 , 38.1 ]

cat("Trimmed observations:", ps_trim$trimmed, "\n")
#> Trimmed observations: 2

7 Key Principles

  1. Full-sample PS, used as-is within subgroups. Propensity scores are estimated once on the entire df.analysis and never re-estimated within subgroup slices. The PS is a design quantity reflecting the treatment assignment mechanism of the study.

  2. IPS covariate, not raw PS. Following Bang & Robins (2005), the IPS covariate \(1/\hat{e}(X)\) for treated and \(1/(1-\hat{e}(X))\) for controls gives the doubly-robust property. A raw PS covariate would be standard covariate adjustment without the DR guarantee.

  3. Bootstrap re-estimates PS. When forestsearch() is called on bootstrap-resampled data, it re-enters Section 2C and re-estimates the propensity score from scratch. This correctly replicates the full estimation procedure.

  4. PS trimming before IPS construction. Extreme PS values are trimmed at [2.5%, 97.5%] before computing the IPS covariate. This prevents numerical instability from near-zero denominators.

  5. GRF is the default PS estimator for observational data because it is (a) non-parametric, (b) cross-fitted via OOB, and

    1. already computed when use_grf = TRUE.

  6. RCTs skip PS by default. When is.RCT = TRUE, ps_method resolves to "none". The user can override this with ps_method = "grf" for precision gains via covariate adjustment, which is permissible under FDA/EMA guidance.

8 References

  • Bang H, Robins JM (2005). “Doubly Robust Estimation in Missing Data and Causal Inference Models.” Biometrics 61(4): 962–973.

  • León LF, Jemielita T, Guo Z, Marceau West R, Anderson KM (2024). “Exploratory subgroup identification in the heterogeneous Cox model.” Statistics in Medicine. DOI: 10.1002/sim.10163.

  • Athey S, Tibshirani J, Wager S (2019). “Generalized Random Forests.” Annals of Statistics 47(2): 1148–1178.

  • Robins JM, Rotnitzky A, Zhao LP (1994). “Estimation of Regression Coefficients When Some Regressors Are Not Always Observed.” JASA 89(427): 846–866.
